mainTopic: Liability for a בור according to רבה and רב יוסף, נחוניא the well-digger, and God's exact judgment of צדיקים
overview: The amud continues the argument between רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא about who is liable for a בור. According to רבה, they argue about a pit on one's own property: רבי עקיבא reads "בעל הבור" as a pit that has an owner, while רבי ישמעאל reads it as the one who made the hazard. רב יוסף disagrees. He says everyone holds a person liable for a pit on private property, and the real argument is about a pit in רשות הרבים. There, רבי ישמעאל learns liability from the words "opens" and "digs", while רבי עקיבא says both words are needed for other lessons. Two ברייתות are brought to challenge the readings, and each time the גמרא shows how both רבה and רב יוסף can explain them. Next, a ברייתא teaches that someone who digs a well and hands it over to the public is exempt, and נחוניא the well-digger is praised for doing exactly that. The amud ends with stories and lessons about how exactly הקדוש ברוך הוא judges צדיקים, and a new teaching on a פסוק that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבה: רבי עקיבא holds a pit in one's own property also makes him liable
steps.stepSummary: Continuing רבה's explanation, the argument is about a pit on one's own property. רבי עקיבא says the owner is liable there too, because the Torah says "בעל הבור", a pit that has an owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: They argue about a pit on his own property. רבי עקיבא holds that a pit on his own property also makes him liable, as it is written "the owner of the pit". The Torah is talking about a pit that has an owner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רבה's explanation of where רבי עקיבא and רבי ישמעאל disagree, and gives רבי עקיבא's view and its source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה places the argument in the case of a בור ברשותו, a pit on one's own land. רבי עקיבא reads "בעל הבור" literally: the Torah speaks of a pit that has an owner. So even a privately owned pit brings liability, and not only a pit in the public domain.

keyTerms.meaning: A pit dug on one's own property
"The owner of the pit", from the פסוק in שמות 21:34
"The Merciful One", a name for ה׳ as the One who wrote the Torah

phrases.english: [they argue] about a pit on his own property –
Rabbi Akiva holds:
a pit on his own property also makes him liable,
as it is written: "The owner of the pit" –
about a pit that has an owner
the Merciful One is speaking,

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא סָבַר: בּוֹר בִּרְשׁוּתוֹ נָמֵי חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבה's explanation from just before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבה, רבי עקיבא holds the owner is liable even for a pit on his own property, learned from "בעל הבור", a pit that has an owner.

steps.title: רבה: רבי ישמעאל reads the verse as the one responsible for the hazard
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל reads "בעל הבור" differently. It means "the one responsible for the hazard", not literal ownership of the pit.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי ישמעאל holds: "the owner of the pit" means the owner of the hazard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the other side of רבה's explanation: how רבי ישמעאל reads the same words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי ישמעאל, "בעל" does not mean owning the pit. It means the person who caused the hazard. So the פסוק does not teach liability for a pit on one's own property. Both sides use the same two words but read them in two ways.

keyTerms.meaning: The one responsible for the hazard, the person who made the obstacle

steps.confusionAlert: Both רבי עקיבא and רבי ישמעאל use the exact same words, "בעל הבור". They do not argue about the פסוק's text. They argue about what "בעל" means here: owner of the pit, or the one who caused the hazard.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yishmael holds:
[it means] the one responsible for the hazard.

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבה: רבי עקיבא reads "בעל הבור" as a pit that has an owner, so a private pit makes him liable. רבי ישמעאל reads it as the one who made the hazard.
steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל סָבַר: בַּעַל הַתַּקָּלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing reading of the same פסוק discussed in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבה, רבי ישמעאל reads "בעל הבור" as "the one responsible for the hazard", not as liability for a pit on one's own property.

steps.title: What does רבי עקיבא mean by 'This is the pit stated in the Torah'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבה explains רבי עקיבא's words in the ברייתא, "זהו בור האמור בתורה". Those words sound as if only this case is the Torah's pit.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then what does רבי עקיבא mean when he says "this is the pit stated in the Torah"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבה's explanation using רבי עקיבא's own wording. It sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא called the pit on one's own property "the pit stated in the Torah". That sounds like it is the only pit the Torah makes him liable for. But by רבה's explanation, רבי עקיבא holds a person liable in every case, including a pit in the public domain. So what is the point of that phrase?

keyTerms.meaning: "But then what...?", a question that pushes back on what was just said
"This is the pit stated in the Torah", רבי עקיבא's words in the ברייתא

phrases.english: But then what is "This is the pit stated in the Torah"
that Rabbi Akiva says?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מַאי זֶהוּ בּוֹר הָאָמוּר בַּתּוֹרָה דְּקָאָמַר רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבה's explanation of רבי עקיבא from step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's claim that רבי עקיבא holds a person liable for a pit in every case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Calling the private-property pit "the pit stated in the Torah" sounds exclusive, as if only this pit brings liability. That does not fit רבה's view that רבי עקיבא makes him liable for a public-domain pit too.

steps.title: It means the pit the Torah mentions first for payment
steps.stepSummary: The phrase does not mean "the only pit". It means this is the pit the פסוק opens with first when it talks about payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the pit the פסוק first begins with regarding payment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by giving a new meaning to רבי עקיבא's phrase.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "זהו בור האמור בתורה" is not limiting. It points to the case the פסוק first opens with when it talks about payment ("בעל הבור ישלם"). So רבה's explanation stands: רבי עקיבא holds him liable for this pit and for a pit in the public domain too.

phrases.english: This is the pit with which
the verse first opened regarding payment.
phrases.notes: He means this is the pit the Torah talks about first, not the only pit that brings liability.

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבה, "זהו בור האמור בתורה" means "the first pit the Torah talks about for payment". It does not mean "the only pit".
steps.triggerLanguage: זֶהוּ בּוֹר שֶׁפָּתַח בּוֹ הַכָּתוּב תְּחִלָּה לְתַשְׁלוּמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: "This is the pit stated in the Torah" seemed to mean this is the only pit that brings liability.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means this is the pit the Torah first discusses for payment, so רבי עקיבא can still hold him liable in other cases too.

steps.title: רב יוסף: everyone agrees a pit on private property makes him liable
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף gives a different explanation from רבה. For a pit on private property, both תנאים agree he is liable, because "בעל הבור" means a pit that has an owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יוסף said: about a pit on private property, everyone agrees that he is liable. What is the reason? The Torah said "the owner of the pit", so we are dealing with a pit that has an owner.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף starts a new explanation of the argument between רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא. Here he first tells us where they do not argue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה said the argument is about a pit on one's own property. רב יוסף says that case is agreed by all: he is liable, from "בעל הבור", a pit with an owner. So the argument must be about some other case, which the גמרא will explain next.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees; literally, "all the world does not argue"

steps.whyThisMatters: רב יוסף moves the argument away from the private-property pit. Now the reading "a pit that has an owner" is accepted by both תנאים.

phrases.english: And Rav Yosef said:
regarding a pit on private property –
everyone agrees that he is liable,
What is the reason?
The Merciful One said "the owner of the pit" –
we are dealing with a pit that has an owner.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב יוֹסֵף אָמַר: בְּבוֹר בִּרְשׁוּת הַיָּחִיד כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי דְּמִחַיַּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different explanation from רבה's (steps 1-4) of where the תנאים argue.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For a pit on private property, all agree he is liable, because "בעל הבור" refers to a pit that has an owner.

steps.title: Where they really argue: a pit in the public area
steps.stepSummary: According to רב יוסף, the argument is about a pit in רשות הרבים. רבי ישמעאל holds the digger is liable, and he learns this from the two words 'opens' and 'digs' in the פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where do they argue? About a pit in the public area. רבי ישמעאל holds that a pit in the public area also makes him liable. The פסוק says 'if he opens' and 'if he digs'. But if he is liable for just opening a pit, he should surely be liable for digging one! So the extra word teaches that responsibility comes to him through the act of opening or digging, even without owning the ground.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף continues his explanation and tells us exactly where the two תנאים disagree: a pit in רשות הרבים. He then gives רבי ישמעאל's reason for saying the digger is liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If opening a pit already makes a person liable, then writing 'digging' too seems unnecessary, since digging is the bigger act. רבי ישמעאל concludes that the פסוק is teaching that the act itself (opening or digging) creates responsibility. Owning the land is not needed, so even a pit in רשות הרבים counts.

keyTerms.meaning: The public domain, an area that belongs to everyone
Opening: uncovering a pit that was already dug
By way of, through the act of

phrases.english: When they disagree, it is about a pit in the public domain;
רבי ישמעאל holds:
for a pit in the public domain, too, he is liable,
as it is written 'if he opens' and 'if he digs'.
If he is liable for opening,
then for digging, is it not all the more so?
Rather, it is through the act of opening
and through the act of digging that it comes to him.
phrases.notes: 'It' means the responsibility for the pit. It comes from what he did, not from owning the ground.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי פְּלִיגִי – בְּבוֹר בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב יוסף's explanation by showing where the argument actually lies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רב יוסף, רבי ישמעאל holds that one is liable for a pit in רשות הרבים. He learns this from the extra words 'opens' and 'digs'.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: both words are needed, first reason
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא says the words 'opens' and 'digs' are not extra. If the Torah wrote only 'opens', we would think a digger must fill the pit in completely, not just cover it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא answers that both words are needed. If the Torah wrote only 'if he opens', I would think that only an opener can free himself by covering the pit. A digger, I would think, cannot get off with just a cover; he must fill the pit in completely.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how רבי עקיבא answers רבי ישמעאל's proof. It shows why the word 'opens' alone would not have been enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל's proof depended on one of the words being extra. רבי עקיבא shows that each word teaches something about how much the person must do to fix the danger. Without 'digs', we would have made the digger's duty stricter than just covering the pit.

keyTerms.meaning: They are truly needed (neither word is extra)
The Merciful One, a name for G-d as the Torah's author
I would have said / I would have thought
Packs it, fills the pit in completely

phrases.english: And רבי עקיבא: these words are needed;
phrases.notes: רבי עקיבא means that 'opens' and 'digs' each teach something, so neither is extra.

phrases.english: for if the Merciful One had written only 'if he opens',
I would have said:
it is the one who opens for whom a covering is enough,
but for the one who digs, a covering is not enough
until he fills it in.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא – הָנְהוּ מִיצְרָךְ צְרִיכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי ישמעאל's proof from step 6 on behalf of רבי עקיבא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the supposedly extra word is needed for a different lesson.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With only 'opens' written, a digger would need to fill in the pit completely.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Digs' is written to teach that a covering is enough for a digger too.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: both words are needed, second reason
steps.stepSummary: If the Torah wrote only 'digs', we would think an opener does not even need to cover the pit, because he did no real action. So both words are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the Torah wrote only 'if he digs', I would think that only digging requires a cover, because the digger did an action. But someone who only opened a pit did no action, so I might think he does not even need to cover it. That is why the Torah wrote both words.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רבי עקיבא's answer. It shows why the word 'digs' alone would not have been enough either.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word blocks a different mistake. 'Digs' stops us from making the digger's duty stricter, and 'opens' stops us from freeing the opener completely. Since neither word is extra, רבי עקיבא has no source for liability on a pit in רשות הרבים. He reads 'בעל הבור' as a pit that has an owner.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches us (that the assumption is wrong)

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב יוסף, רבי ישמעאל uses 'opens' and 'digs' to make a person liable even for a public pit. רבי עקיבא says both words are needed to teach that covering works for both the opener and the digger. So for רבי עקיבא, only an owned pit is included.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא ״כִּי יִכְרֶה״ – הֲוָה אָמֵינָא:
phrases.english: And if the Merciful One had written only 'if he digs', I would have said:
it is digging that requires a covering,
because he did an action;
but the one who opens, who did not do an action,
say he does not even need a covering;
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא ״כִּי יִכְרֶה״ – הֲוָה אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-sided explanation begun in step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Second half of the explanation that both words are needed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With only 'digs' written, an opener would not even need to cover the pit.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both words are needed, so neither is extra, and there is no source for a public pit according to רבי עקיבא.

steps.title: How does רב יוסף explain 'this is the Torah's pit'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבי ישמעאל meant by 'זהו בור האמור בתורה'. According to רב יוסף, a pit on one's own property is also a Torah pit, so this pit is not the only one.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then what does רבי ישמעאל mean when he says 'this is the pit stated in the Torah'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב יוסף from the wording of the ברייתא. This is the same kind of question it asked רבה in step 3.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, רבי ישמעאל calls the public pit 'the pit stated in the Torah'. That sounds as if only the public pit counts. But רב יוסף said both תנאים agree that a pit on private property also makes a person liable.

keyTerms.meaning: But then what is meant by...?
This is the pit stated in the Torah

steps.confusionAlert: In step 3 this phrase was asked about as רבי עקיבא's words, according to רבה. Here, according to רב יוסף, the same phrase is רבי ישמעאל's.

phrases.english: But then what is 'this is the pit stated in the Torah'
that רבי ישמעאל says?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֶלָּא מַאי ״זֶהוּ בּוֹר הָאָמוּר בַּתּוֹרָה״ דְּקָאָמַר רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests רב יוסף's explanation against the wording of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's claim that a pit on private property is also a Torah pit according to both תנאים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Calling the public pit 'the pit stated in the Torah' suggests it is the only one.

steps.title: It is the first pit the פסוק mentions
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל's phrase means that the public pit is the one the פסוק opens with when it starts discussing damages. It does not mean it is the only pit.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the pit that the פסוק talks about first when it begins discussing damages.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by reading the phrase as 'the first pit', just as it did for רבה in step 4.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'כי יפתח' and 'כי יכרה' come first and refer to a public pit. Only afterward does the פסוק say 'בעל הבור', which refers to a pit that has an owner. So both kinds are included, and רב יוסף's explanation stands.
steps.whatToRemember: For both רבה and רב יוסף, 'זהו בור האמור בתורה' means 'the first pit the פסוק mentions', not 'the only pit'.

phrases.english: This is the pit with which the פסוק opens
first regarding damages.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶהוּ בּוֹר שֶׁפָּתַח בּוֹ הַכָּתוּב תְּחִלָּה לִנְזָקִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereads the wording: 'this is' means 'first', not 'only'.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase seemed to mean the public pit is the only pit.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is simply the first pit the פסוק mentions. The owned pit comes afterward with 'בעל הבור'.

steps.title: A ברייתא: pit under the street, opening into private property
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to test the argument. Its first case is a pit whose hollow is under the public domain but whose opening is in private property. The digger is exempt, even though digging under the street is not allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: One who digs a pit in the public domain and opens it into private property is exempt. This is so even though he is not allowed to do this, because one may not make a hollow under the public domain.
steps.whatsHappening: The word מיתיבי tells us the גמרא is bringing a source that may contradict what was just said. This step quotes the first case of that source; the actual challenge comes a few steps later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The hollow of the pit is under the street, but the opening, where an animal would fall in, is in private property. The ברייתא says he is exempt for damages. It adds that digging under the street is still forbidden, because one may not make a hollow under the public domain.

keyTerms.meaning: They challenged: the גמרא is bringing a source that seems to contradict what was said
Exempt, does not have to pay

steps.confusionAlert: "Exempt" here only means he does not pay for damages. It does not mean digging under the street is allowed. The ברייתא says clearly that it is not allowed.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
One who digs a pit in the public domain,
phrases.notes: He means the hollow part of the pit is under the street.

phrases.english: and opens it into private property, is exempt;

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ רַשַּׁאי לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן,
phrases.english: even though he is not permitted to do so,

phrases.aramaic: לְפִי שֶׁאֵין עוֹשִׂין חָלָל תַּחַת רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים.
phrases.english: because one may not make a hollow under the public domain.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After explaining רב יוסף's reading of רבי ישמעאל, the גמרא brings a ברייתא to test the two readings.
steps.kashyaTarget: The readings of the argument between רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא, especially רב יוסף's
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's rulings will be checked against each reading to see which תנא they fit. The full challenge is built in the next steps.

steps.title: More cases: pit opening onto the street, and pits dug for foundations
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. A pit dug in private property that opens onto the street makes the digger liable. A pit dug in private property next to the street for foundations is exempt. רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה makes him liable unless he puts up a ten-handbreadth wall or keeps the pit four handbreadths away from where people and animals walk.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who digs pits, ditches, or caves in private property and opens them onto the public domain is liable. One who digs pits in private property that is next to the public domain, like those who dig for foundations, is exempt. רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה makes him liable unless he builds a wall ten handbreadths high, or keeps it four handbreadths away from where people and animals walk.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is still quoting the ברייתא. It adds the opposite case and a case of digging next to the street.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the opening faces the street, people and animals can fall in, so he is liable. Digging foundations next to the street is a normal, accepted thing to do, so the תנא קמא exempts him. רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה says he must still protect people, either with a wall or by keeping a distance.

keyTerms.meaning: Foundations dug for a house or wall

phrases.aramaic: הַחוֹפֵר בּוֹרוֹת, שִׁיחִין וּמְעָרוֹת בִּרְשׁוּת הַיָּחִיד,
phrases.english: One who digs pits, ditches, and caves in private property,
and opens it onto the public domain, is liable.
And one who digs pits in private property
that is next to the public domain,
such as those who dig for foundations, is exempt.
But רבי יוסי son of רבי יהודה holds him liable
unless he builds a partition ten handbreadths high,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ עַד שֶׁיַּרְחִיק מִמְּקוֹם דְּרִיסַת רַגְלֵי אָדָם
phrases.english: or unless he distances it from the place where people walk

phrases.aramaic: וּמִמְּקוֹם דְּרִיסַת רַגְלֵי בְהֵמָה – אַרְבָּעָה טְפָחִים.
phrases.english: and from the place where animals walk, four handbreadths.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַחוֹפֵר בּוֹרוֹת, שִׁיחִין וּמְעָרוֹת בִּרְשׁוּת הַיָּחִיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues quoting the same ברייתא with more cases.
steps.kashyaTarget: The readings of the argument between רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: These cases supply the material for the inference in the next step about a pit dug in one's own property.

steps.title: Inference: digging next to the street for any other purpose makes one liable
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads between the lines of the ברייתא. The exemption is only because he dug for foundations. If he dug for another reason, he would be liable, even though the pit is in his own property.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason he is exempt is that he dug for foundations. But if not for foundations, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a hidden rule out of the ברייתא's words "for foundations".
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא only exempted foundation-digging, which is normal and needed. So a pit dug in one's own property, next to where people walk, for any other reason makes him liable. This shows that a pit in one's own property can make a person liable.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason: the גמרא is pinpointing why the ruling is so
But if not: introduces the opposite case that we infer

steps.whyThisMatters: This inference is the key fact the גמרא will test against רבה and רב יוסף: liability for a pit in one's own property.

phrases.english: The reason is that it was for foundations,
but if not for foundations, he is liable;

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא דִּלְאוּשִּׁין, הָא לָאו לְאוּשִּׁין – חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from the foundations case just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: Which תנא holds that a pit in one's own property makes a person liable
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the ברייתא holds that a pit in one's own property brings liability, we must find a תנא who holds this, and then see whether each reading of the argument fits.

steps.title: Whose view is the ברייתא? It fits רבה easily
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which Tanna the ברייתא follows. According to רבה, the answer is easy: the first clause is רבי ישמעאל and the last clause is רבי עקיבא. This sets up the coming problem for רב יוסף.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view is this? It works well according to רבה: the first clause is רבי ישמעאל, and the last clause is רבי עקיבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks who wrote the ברייתא. It shows that רבה's reading fits it, which prepares the next move: asking how it fits רב יוסף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבה, the two תנאים argue about a pit in one's own property. רבי ישמעאל exempts, and that matches the first clause, where the opening is in private property and he is exempt. רבי עקיבא holds him liable, and that matches the last clause, where digging in one's own property for something other than foundations makes him liable.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted, it works well: sets up a contrast with a view that has trouble

steps.confusionAlert: בשלמא means "this one works." It is a hint that the next view, רב יוסף's, is about to run into trouble.

phrases.english: Whose view is this?
Granted, according to רבה,
the first clause is רבי ישמעאל,
and the last clause is רבי עקיבא.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא מַנִּי? בִּשְׁלָמָא לְרַבָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the inference from step 13 to identify the ברייתא's author. It shows the fit with רבה before turning to רב יוסף.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא or תנאים the ברייתא follows, and whether it fits רבה and רב יוסף
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: According to רבה, the first clause follows רבי ישמעאל and the last clause follows רבי עקיבא. Step 15 raises the problem for רב יוסף, and step 16 answers it.

steps.title: According to רב יוסף, the first clause seems to match no one
steps.stepSummary: For רב יוסף, the last clause works for everyone, but the first clause (a digger exempt for a pit opening into his own property) seems to fit neither רבי ישמעאל nor רבי עקיבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to רב יוסף: fine, the last clause is everyone's view. But whose view is the first clause? It is not רבי ישמעאל's and it is not רבי עקיבא's!
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא turns to רב יוסף and challenges him. His reading seems to leave the first clause of the ברייתא without any תנא who agrees with it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב יוסף, both רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא hold that a person is liable for a pit on his own property, even if he later gives up the property. The first clause exempts a digger whose pit opens into his own property. So that exemption seems to go against both of them.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted, this part works fine (used to set up a contrast with a part that does not)
The last clause of a teaching
The first clause of a teaching

phrases.english: But according to Rav Yosef,
granted, the last clause is the view of everyone;
but the first clause, whose view is it?
phrases.notes: That's the first case from step 11: the hollow is under the street, but the opening is on his own property, and he is exempt.

phrases.aramaic: לָא רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל, וְלָא רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא!
phrases.english: Not Rabbi Yishmael and not Rabbi Akiva!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לְרַב יוֹסֵף, בִּשְׁלָמָא סֵיפָא – דִּבְרֵי הַכֹּל; אֶלָּא רֵישָׁא מַנִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 14 showed that רבה can explain the ברייתא. This step shows the problem that creates for רב יוסף.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's explanation of the dispute between רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In רב יוסף's view, both תנאים make a person liable for a pit on his own property. But the first clause of the ברייתא exempts such a digger, so no תנא is left who agrees with it.

steps.title: רב יוסף: the first clause is about someone who gave up nothing
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that the whole ברייתא is agreed by everyone. The first clause is about a person who never gave up ownership of his property or his pit.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף can tell you: the whole ברייתא is everyone's view. The first clause is talking about someone who did not give up ownership of his property and did not give up ownership of his pit.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף defends himself. He says the first clause is a different kind of case, so it does not go against anyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב יוסף, the agreed rule that he is liable covers a person who gave up his property but kept his pit. The real dispute is about a pit in the public domain (step 6). In the first clause, the digger gave up nothing, so the opening is simply inside his own private property, and everyone agrees he is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: He can tell you (introduces how someone would answer the challenge)
All of it, the whole teaching
He gave up ownership, making it ownerless

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רב יוסף changed his view that an owner is liable for a pit on his own property. That rule is about someone who gave up ownership. Here the digger gave up nothing, so it is a different case.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef can say to you:
the whole of it is the view of everyone,
and the first clause is where he did not give up ownership of
neither his property nor his pit.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לְךָ רַב יוֹסֵף: כּוּלַּהּ דִּבְרֵי הַכֹּל הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case in the first clause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first clause seemed to be a person who gave up his property, which רב יוסף holds makes everyone say he is liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first clause is a person who gave up nothing. His pit is just in his own property, and everyone agrees he is exempt.

steps.title: רב אשי: רבה does not need to split the ברייתא either
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says that since רב יוסף can read the whole ברייתא as everyone's view, רבה also does not have to split it between two תנאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Now that you explained the ברייתא as everyone's view according to רב יוסף, you also do not need to explain it as a split between תנאים according to רבה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי makes a new suggestion about how רבה reads the ברייתא. This line sets up his explanation, which comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 14, רבה's reading made the first clause follow רבי ישמעאל and the last clause follow רבי עקיבא. רב אשי thinks it is better not to split one ברייתא between two opinions. He will show that רבה can read the whole thing as one opinion.

keyTerms.meaning: Now that (introduces a point that follows from what was just said)
You established it, you explained it as being about

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Now that you have explained it, according to Rav Yosef,
as the view of everyone,
according to Rabba too, do not explain it as a dispute between Tannaim.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: הַשְׁתָּא דְּאוֹקֵימְתַּהּ לְרַב יוֹסֵף לְדִבְרֵי הַכֹּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רב יוסף's one-opinion reading from step 16 to go back and improve רבה's reading from step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבה also does not need to split the ברייתא between two תנאים.

steps.title: The whole ברייתא follows רבי ישמעאל
steps.stepSummary: Both clauses follow רבי ישמעאל. The 'liable' case read into the last clause is someone who widened his pit out into the public domain.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the first clause is רבי ישמעאל, the last clause is also רבי ישמעאל. The reason he is exempt is that he dug for foundations. If not for foundations, he is liable. That is, for example, where he widened the pit out into the public domain.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי explains how רבה can read the whole ברייתא as רבי ישמעאל. He reinterprets the 'he would be liable' case that the גמרא read into the ברייתא in step 13.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 13, the גמרא read the last clause to mean that a person digging in his own property for a reason other than foundations is liable, which seemed to go against רבי ישמעאל. רב אשי says that liable case is not a pit in his own property. It is a pit he widened into the street, which is a pit in the public domain, so even רבי ישמעאל agrees he is liable.
steps.whatToRemember: Both רב יוסף and רבה can read the whole ברייתא as one view. For רב יוסף, the first clause is someone who gave up nothing. For רבה, as רב אשי explains, the whole ברייתא is רבי ישמעאל, and the liable case is a pit widened into the street.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the ברייתא does not decide between רבה and רב יוסף. Each one can explain it without splitting it.

phrases.english: Since the first clause is Rabbi Yishmael,
the last clause is also Rabbi Yishmael;
and the reason is that he dug for foundations,
but if not for foundations, he is liable
such as where he widened it out into the public domain.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִדְּרֵישָׁא רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל, סֵיפָא נָמֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the claim made in step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case read into the last clause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'liable' case read into the last clause meant a pit dug inside his own property for another reason, which goes against רבי ישמעאל.
steps.terutzMaskana: The liable case is a pit widened into the public domain, where even רבי ישמעאל makes him liable. So the whole ברייתא follows רבי ישמעאל.

steps.title: A new ברייתא about a pit opening into the public domain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא: digging in private property with the opening in the public domain makes you liable, but digging in private property next to the public domain makes you exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: One who digs a pit on private property and opens it into the public domain is liable. If he digs on private property that is next to the public domain, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to test the two views from before. This step only quotes the source. The actual challenge comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא has two clauses. If the opening faces the public, he is liable. If the pit is only next to the public area, he is exempt. Each clause will be checked against רבה and רב יוסף.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection (from a תנאי source)

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
One who digs a pit on private property
and opens it into the public domain is liable.

phrases.aramaic: בִּרְשׁוּת הַיָּחִיד הַסְּמוּכָה לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: On private property that is next to the public domain, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new outside source to test the רבה and רב יוסף dispute again.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Pit dug on private property with its opening in the public domain makes him liable. Pit on private property next to the public domain makes him exempt.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's explanation of the dispute between רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא exempts a pit on private property next to the public domain. The next step checks whether that exemption can fit any תנא according to רב יוסף.

steps.title: The last clause seems to fit no תנא for רב יוסף
steps.stepSummary: For רבה the whole ברייתא is רבי ישמעאל. For רב יוסף the first clause is רבי ישמעאל, but the exempt last clause seems to fit neither רבי ישמעאל nor רבי עקיבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, according to רבה, the whole ברייתא is רבי ישמעאל. But according to רב יוסף, granted the first clause is רבי ישמעאל. But whose view is the last clause? It is neither רבי ישמעאל nor רבי עקיבא!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב יוסף. Under his reading, the exempt ruling in the last clause does not match any known תנא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה can read both clauses as one consistent view, רבי ישמעאל. רב יוסף's understanding of the תנאים leaves the exemption in the סיפא without a source. So רב יוסף seems to be contradicted.

phrases.english: Granted, according to Rabba,
all of it is Rabbi Yishmael.
But according to Rav Yosef,
granted, the first clause is Rabbi Yishmael,
but whose view is the last clause?

phrases.aramaic: לָא רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל וְלָא רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא!
phrases.english: Not Rabbi Yishmael and not Rabbi Akiva!

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְרַבָּה, כּוּלַּהּ רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל הִיא. אֶלָּא לְרַב יוֹסֵף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the ברייתא just quoted to attack רב יוסף.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's understanding of the dispute between רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under רב יוסף's reading, the exemption in the last clause matches no known תנא. That makes his reading hard to accept.

steps.title: The last clause is about digging for foundations
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that the exempt case is someone digging for building foundations. In that case everyone agrees he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: He can say to you: It is about someone digging for foundations, and that is everyone's view.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב יוסף. It narrows the last clause to a special case that all the תנאים agree on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exempt clause is not about an ordinary pit. It is about a person digging to lay the foundations of a building. So it does not need to match one side of the dispute, since everyone agrees.
steps.whatToRemember: With the foundations answer, both רבה and רב יוסף survive the ברייתא.

phrases.english: He can say to you:
It is about one who digs for foundations,
and it is everyone's view.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא against רב יוסף.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The last clause is about an ordinary pit, so it must follow one side of the dispute.
steps.terutzMaskana: The last clause is about digging for foundations, which everyone agrees is exempt.

steps.title: Handing a dug well over to the public
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches: if he dug, opened and handed the well over to the public, he is exempt. If he did not hand it over, he is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: If he dug, opened, and handed it over to the public, he is exempt. If he dug and opened but did not hand it over to the public, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a ברייתא about a person who digs wells for the public.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key factor is handing the well over. Once it belongs to the public, he is no longer responsible for damage it causes. If he keeps it, the pit is still his and he stays liable.

keyTerms.meaning: Handed it over to the public

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
If he dug and opened and handed it over to the public, he is exempt.

phrases.aramaic: חָפַר וּפָתַח וְלֹא מָסַר לָרַבִּים – חַיָּיב,
phrases.english: If he dug and opened and did not hand it over to the public, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: חָפַר וּפָתַח וּמָסַר לָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new related topic about responsibility for dug pits.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Handing a dug well over to the public exempts the digger. Not handing it over leaves him liable.

steps.title: נחוניא the well-digger followed this rule
steps.stepSummary: נחוניא used to dig wells and hand them over to the public. When the חכמים heard, they said he fulfilled this הלכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this was the practice of נחוניא, the digger of pits, ditches and caves. He would dig, open, and hand them over to the public. When the חכמים heard about it, they said: This man has fulfilled this הלכה.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a real-life example of the rule from נחוניא, and the חכמים praise him for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נחוניא dug water sources for the public and was careful to hand them over. That way he was not responsible for damage they caused. The חכמים' words show his practice was the correct way to act.

keyTerms.meaning: נחוניא the ditch-digger, who dug water sources for the public
Ditches and caves (kinds of water pits)

phrases.english: And this was the practice of Neḥunya,
the digger of pits, ditches, and caves,
that he would dig, open, and hand them over to the public.
And when the Sages heard about the matter,
they said: This one has fulfilled this halakha.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן מִנְהָגוֹ שֶׁל נְחוּנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the rule from step 22 being put into practice.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that handing a well over to the public exempts the digger
steps.raayaSupportSource: נחוניא's practice and the חכמים' approval of it

steps.title: Only this one הלכה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: did נחוניא fulfill only this one הלכה and nothing more?
steps.simpleTranslation: This הלכה and nothing more?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of the חכמים' praise. It sounds like נחוניא kept only this one rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying "he fulfilled this הלכה" seems to suggest he kept nothing else. That cannot be said about a person like נחוניא, so the wording needs fixing.

phrases.english: This halakha and nothing more?!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲלָכָה זוֹ וְתוּ לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the חכמים' praise in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase קיים זה הלכה זו
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The wording implies נחוניא kept only one הלכה, which is not a fitting thing to say about him.

steps.title: Read it as "even this הלכה"
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא fixes the wording: the חכמים said he fulfilled even this הלכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: Even this הלכה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by adjusting the words of the praise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Adding the word "even" changes the meaning. נחוניא kept all the מצוות, and he was careful about this detailed rule too.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
even this halakha.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording question of step 24.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He fulfilled only this one הלכה.
steps.terutzMaskana: He fulfilled even this הלכה, on top of everything else.

steps.title: נחוניא's daughter falls into a pit
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells that נחוניא's daughter fell into a large pit. רבי חנינא בן דוסא was told. After the first and second hours he said "peace," and after the third he said "she has come up."
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: There was a story with the daughter of נחוניא the ditch-digger, who fell into a large pit. They came and told רבי חנינא בן דוסא. In the first hour he said to them: Peace. In the second he said to them: Peace. In the third he said to them: She has come up.
steps.whatsHappening: Since נחוניא was just mentioned, the גמרא tells a story about his daughter and רבי חנינא בן דוסא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a story section, not a legal argument. Hour after hour, רבי חנינא בן דוסא calmly tells the people that she is safe, and at the end he says she has come up.

keyTerms.meaning: A story, an incident that happened
A תנא famous for his righteousness

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: There was an incident
with the daughter of Neḥunya the ditch-digger,
who fell into a large pit.

phrases.aramaic: בָּאוּ וְהוֹדִיעוּ אֶת רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא.
phrases.english: They came and informed Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa.
In the first hour he said to them: Peace.
phrases.notes: He means she is safe and unharmed.

phrases.english: In the second he said to them: Peace.
In the third he said to them: She has come up.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּבִתּוֹ שֶׁל נְחוּנְיָא חוֹפֵר שִׁיחִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues with a story about נחוניא, who was mentioned in step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Story: רבי חנינא בן דוסא calmly reassures the people about נחוניא's daughter until she comes up from the pit.

steps.title: The daughter explains how she was rescued
steps.stepSummary: People ask נחוניא's daughter who pulled her out, and she says a ram appeared, led by an old man.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked her: Who brought you up? She told them: A ram came my way, and an old man was leading it.
steps.whatsHappening: The story from the ברייתא continues. The girl is safely out of the pit, and she describes how she was saved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 26, רבי חנינא בן דוסא announced 'she has come up.' Now we hear it really happened, and it happened in a wondrous way: a ram and a mysterious old man. The story does not say who the old man was.

keyTerms.meaning: brought you up (out of the pit)
a male of the ewes, a ram

phrases.english: They said to her: Who brought you up?

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרָה לָהֶם: זָכָר שֶׁל רְחֵלִים נִזְדַּמֵּן לִי,
phrases.english: She said to them: A male of the ewes happened to come to me,
and a certain old man was leading it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לָהּ: מִי הֶעֱלִךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of step 26 by confirming the girl came up and describing how.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The daughter of נחוניא was rescued in a wondrous way by a ram led by an old man.

steps.title: People ask רבי חנינא בן דוסא if he is a prophet
steps.stepSummary: Since he knew ahead of time that she would come up, people ask רבי חנינא בן דוסא whether he is a prophet.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Are you a prophet?
steps.whatsHappening: The people turn to רבי חנינא בן דוסא and ask how he knew she was safe. This question sets up his answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Back in step 26 he said 'she has come up' before anyone saw it. That looks like prophecy, so they want to know how he could have known.

phrases.english: They said to him: Are you a prophet?
phrases.notes: 'Him' is רבי חנינא בן דוסא from the start of the story.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: נָבִיא אַתָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Since the girl's rescue confirmed his words, they ask how he knew.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How did רבי חנינא בן דוסא know the girl had come up? Was it through prophecy?

steps.title: Not prophecy, but reasoning about a צדיק's merit
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא בן דוסא says he is no prophet. He simply reasoned that a צדיק's children would not be hurt by the very thing he worked so hard for.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: 'I am not a prophet, and I am not a prophet's son.' Rather, this is what I told myself: Should the children of that צדיק stumble through the very thing he worked so hard for?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא בן דוסא answers the question. He knew she would be saved because of logic, not prophecy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נחוניא spent his life digging wells and pits for people to drink from. It would make no sense for his own child to be harmed by a pit. So the girl's rescue came through her father's merit.
steps.whatToRemember: A צדיק's children are protected from harm through the very מצוה the צדיק worked hard on.

phrases.english: He said to them:
"I am not a prophet,
and I am not a prophet's son,"
rather, this is what I said to myself:
a thing that this righteous man worked so hard over,
phrases.notes: 'That righteous man' is נחוניא, and the 'thing' is digging wells and pits for people.

phrases.english: should his children stumble through it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶם: לֹא נָבִיא אָנֹכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He was not prophesying. He reasoned that נחוניא's child would not be harmed by the very wells he dug for others.

steps.title: Even so, נחוניא's son died of thirst
steps.stepSummary: רבי אחא says that even so, נחוניא's son died of thirst, because God is exact with the righteous even to a hair's breadth.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אחא said: Even so, his son died of thirst. As the פסוק says: 'And around Him it storms greatly.' This teaches that הקדוש ברוך הוא is exacting with those close to Him, even to a hair's breadth.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אחא adds a surprising and painful twist: despite all of נחוניא's merit, his son died of thirst. He brings a פסוק to explain why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word נִשְׂעֲרָה ('storms') sounds like שַׂעֲרָה ('a hair'). So the פסוק is read as: with those around Him, God is exact down to a hair. Being close to God does not mean being let off easily; it means being judged more precisely.

keyTerms.meaning: those around Him, the righteous who are close to God
is exact, careful about every detail
like a strand of hair, to a hair's breadth

steps.confusionAlert: This does not contradict step 29. The daughter was saved by her father's merit, but the son still died, because God judges צדיקים with extreme exactness. Both ideas stand side by side.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a key idea: being righteous earns protection, but it also means being held to a much higher, more precise standard.

phrases.english: Rabbi Acha said:

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי כֵן, מֵת בְּנוֹ בַּצָּמָא.
phrases.english: Even so, his son died of thirst.
phrases.notes: 'His son' means נחוניא's son, the same man who dug water wells for everyone.

phrases.english: as it is said: "And around Him it storms greatly"
phrases.notes: תהלים 50:3. The word for 'storms' sounds like the word for 'hair', and that is the key to the lesson.

phrases.english: this teaches that the Holy One, Blessed be He,
is exacting with those around Him
even to the width of a strand of hair.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַחָא: אַף עַל פִּי כֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the happy ending, adds that נחוניא's son still died, and explains why from a פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: הקדוש ברוך הוא is exacting with the righteous even to a hair's breadth, so נחוניא's son still died of thirst.

steps.title: A second פסוק for the same idea
steps.stepSummary: רבי נחוניא learns the same idea, that God is exact with those close to Him, from a different פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי נחוניא said: We learn it from here: 'A God dreaded in the great council of the holy ones, and feared by all those around Him.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי נחוניא gives a different source for רבי אחא's lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea stays the same: God is exact with the righteous. Only the source changes. This פסוק says God is 'feared by all those around Him,' meaning those closest to Him are judged most strictly.

keyTerms.meaning: in the council of the holy ones

phrases.english: Rabbi Nechunya said: from here:
"A God dreaded in the great council of the holy ones,
and feared by all those around Him."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי נְחוּנְיָא אָמַר מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different פסוק as the source for the lesson of step 30.
steps.raayaObject: That God is exact with the righteous who are close to Him.
steps.raayaSupportSource: תהלים 89:8: 'and feared by all those around Him.'

steps.title: Never say God simply lets things go
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא warns that anyone who says God overlooks wrongdoing will have his own life 'let go,' because all of God's ways are justice.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said: Anyone who says that הקדוש ברוך הוא lets things go, his life will be let go. As the פסוק says: 'The Rock, His work is perfect, for all His ways are justice.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא continues the theme of God's exact judgment with a strong warning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a play on words: וַתְּרָן ('one who lets things go') and יִוָּתְרוּ ('will be let go'). Someone who thinks God ignores sins is wrong, because the פסוק says all His ways are justice. God may be patient, but He does not simply cancel what is due.

keyTerms.meaning: one who gives in, lets things slide
his life will be given up, let go
the Rock, a name for God

steps.whatToRemember: God's judgment is perfectly fair and exact; He does not simply ignore wrongdoing.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הָאוֹמֵר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וַתְּרָן הוּא,
phrases.english: Anyone who says the Holy One, Blessed be He, is one who lets things go,
his life will be let go,
as it is said: "The Rock, His work is perfect,
for all His ways are justice."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: כׇּל הָאוֹמֵר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וַתְּרָן הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the theme of God's exact judgment from steps 30-31.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may not say God overlooks sin; all His ways are justice.

steps.title: Opening a question about a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנא (or, some say, רבי שמואל בר נחמני) begins to ask what a certain פסוק means.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנא said, and some say it was רבי שמואל בר נחמני: What is the meaning of what is written:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is opening a new teaching about a פסוק, and the פסוק itself comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two opinions about who said this teaching: רבי חנא or רבי שמואל בר נחמני. The phrase 'מאי דכתיב' tells us a פסוק is about to be explained, most likely continuing the theme of how God judges.

keyTerms.meaning: and some say (it was someone else who said this)
what is the meaning of what is written

phrases.english: Rabbi Chana said,
and some say it was Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani,
What is the meaning of that which is written:
phrases.notes: The פסוק he is asking about comes right after this, on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חָנָא וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי, מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new teaching about a פסוק that continues the theme of God's judgment.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of a פסוק that is quoted in the continuation of the text.
